1.40.m:
Pulastya said:
Then he created Brahmā, the foremost among the possessors of yoga, of great splendour,
the creator of all worlds, facing in all directions,

in that golden lotus, many yojanas wide,
consisting of all radiant qualities, endowed with earthly characteristics.

And that lotus which arose in the past as the excellent form of the earth,
the great sages declare to have sprung from Nārāyaṇa.

The lotus which is the earth is declared to be the goddess Rasā;
the foremost filaments of that lotus they know to be the divine mountains:

Himavat, Nīla, Meru, and Niṣadha,
Kailāsa, Śṛṅgavat, and likewise Mount Gandhamādana,

the holy Triśikhara, and lovely Mandara,
noble Piñjara, Vindhya, and Mount Asta.

These indeed are the abodes of the Gaṇas, of the Siddhas, and of the great souls
of virtuous character, yielding the fruit of all desires.

Between these lies the continent known as Jambūdvīpa;
the layout of Jambūdvīpa, wherein sacrificial rites are performed.

The water which flows from them, like the essence of divine nectar,
forms lakes on all sides, the receptacles of hundreds of divine tīrthas.

Those filaments of the lotus that are all around,
they are the innumerable and diverse mountains on the earth.

The abundant outer leaves of the lotus, O king,
are proclaimed to be the inaccessible Mleccha lands, packed with mountains.

The leaves on the lower part are the dwelling places, in their respective divisions,
of Daityas, Asuras, and Pannagas, O king.

The space within their midst is known as Rasātala,
where men of heinous deeds sink down.

Four oceans are reckoned in the four cardinal directions;
thus the earth originated from the lotus for Nārāyaṇa.

Therefore, this manifestation is also named Puṣkara.
For this reason, at a sacrifice, by the ancient supreme sages,

the pile for the sacrificial post was built through sacrifices with Vedic examples.
Thus by that blessed one, the earth was arranged, pervading the universe;

and the formation of mountains and rivers was fashioned.
He whose majesty for the universe is matchless, shining like the sun, Varuna of boundless lustre,

the Self-born, composed of the universe, gradually released in the great ocean the treasure of the lotus which was asleep.
An obstacle to tapas arose: a great asura named Madhu,

and born together with him was the asura named Kaiṭabha.
Both were born of rajas and tamas, two hosts of tamasic nature.

The two of great might agitated the entire world, the single ocean,
wearing celestial red garments, with white, blazing, fierce fangs,

exalted with diadems and crowns, shining with armlets and bracelets,
with wide-open copper-coloured eyes, broad chests, and mighty arms,

with the build of a great mountain, like two moving mountains,
resembling fresh clouds, with faces like the sun,

very terrifying with hands adorned with broad armlets,
as if tossing the ocean with the stamping of their feet,

making Hari, the slayer of Madhu, as it were, tremble while sleeping.
Wandering there on that lotus, facing in all directions,

they then saw the foremost among yogis, exceedingly radiant,
instructed by Nārāyaṇa, creating all creatures,

and all the deities, and the sages who are his mind-born sons.
Then those two foremost asuras said to Brahmā there,

wicked, eager to fight, infuriated, their eyes agitated with anger:
'Who are you, seated in the middle of the lotus, with a white turban and four arms?

Ignoring the two of us out of delusion, you sit free from desire.
Come! Come and give us a fight, you lotus-born one!

You are unable to stay in the ocean against us two supreme lords!
Who would be there for you, and by whom have you been appointed here?

Who is your creator, and who is your protector? By what name is he called?'
Brahmā said:
'In the world, the Lord is called Viṣṇu, who wields infinite power.

Know me, the creator, to be born from his presence.'
Madhu and Kaiṭabha said:
'There is nothing in the world supreme to the two of us, O great sage!

The universe is enveloped by us two with darkness and passion.
We are full of rajas and tamas, transcending even the sages.

Concealing righteous conduct, we destroy all embodied beings.
Through age after age, the world is joined with us two, hard to overcome.

We two are wealth and desire, the sacrifice and all possessions,
wherever there is pleasure, wherever intoxication, wherever fortune and fame.'

Consider that whatever is desired by anyone, that is us."
Brahmā said:
"Seeing you two united, who were previously defeated by us,

I have focused upon that virtuous one and taken refuge in sattva—
he who is supreme, whose self is united in yoga, who is imperishable, and who is sattva itself,

and who is the creator of rajas and tamas, the source of the universe.
From him are born the beings that are sāttvika and otherwise.

He alone, Vāsudeva, will bring about your destruction."
Then, while still asleep, the god Nārāyaṇa,

O Brahmā, created by his own māyā arms extending many yojanas.
Then, pulled by his arms, those two possessing mighty arms,

moved about enfeebled, like two fat birds.
Then, having gone there, they spoke to eternal Vāsudeva,

both bowing down, prostrating to the lotus-navelled Hṛṣīkeśa:
"We know you to be the source of the universe, you, the one Supreme Person.

Knowing you to be the cause of us two, the origin of intellect,
since we know you as eternal, true, and of unfailing sight,

therefore, O God, we desire to look upon you completely.
You are of unfailing sight; homage to you, conqueror in battle!"

The Blessed One said:
"Why do you two, best of Asuras, address me thus?
You whose lifespan has expired, do you, alas, wish to live again?"

Madhu and Kaiṭabha said:
"Where no one has ever died, O God, there let our death be, O Lord!
And we wish to be your sons, O you of exceedingly great austerities!"

The Blessed One said:
"Let this be so for you two. In the future Kali age,
you shall surely be [my sons], there is no doubt; I speak this truth to you."

Then, having granted the boon to the two great Asuras, the eternal, universe-sustaining best of gods,
the Lord of immortals, crushed upon his thighs those two born of rajas and tamas, who resembled collyrium.

Standing upon that lotus, Brahmā, the best of the knowers of Brahman,
with arms raised up, of great splendor, undertook fierce austerities.

Blazing, as it were, with his energies, dispelling darkness with his own rays,
that righteous-souled one shone like the thousand-rayed sun with its beams.

Then, assuming another form, the imperishable Lord Nārāyaṇa
came, of great splendor, the master of yoga, possessing great renown,

and the wise Kapila, the master of Sāṅkhya, the best of knowers of Brahman.
Both of those great-souled ones, devoted [to the truth], were worshipped there.

Those two having arrived, who knew the distinction between the higher and the lower and were worshipped by the great seers,
spoke there to Brahmā of immeasurable splendor:

"Brahman is to be known by you; abiding in the vast world,
Brahmā is the leader of all beings, worshipped by the three worlds."

Hearing their word, having been awakened to the supreme state after they departed,
he fashioned these three worlds according to this Vedic revelation of Brahmā.

And he brought forth one son born from himself, [named] Bhū.
Then, before him, there came a mind-born son of Brahmā.

As soon as he was born, that mind-born son said to Brahmā:
"What help shall we give you? Let the Blessed One speak."

Brahmā said:
"Whatever this Kapila by name and Nārāyaṇa, the Brahman,
said to you, O you of great intellect, do that!"

Thus addressed by Brahmā, he who had arisen from the earth said to those two,
with folded hands: "I am eager to serve you two; what shall I do?"

Hearing this speech, he went to the northern direction,
and having gone there, he reached Brahman through the eye of knowledge.

Then the lord Brahmā created a second [son] named Bhuvas,
having fashioned him in his mind alone, the magnanimous one.

Then he also spoke these words: "What shall I do, O Grandfather?"
Instructed by the Grandfather, he approached Brahmā.

The nectar-like essence of Brahman was indeed experienced by him from that;
he reached the supreme state, having come to the side of those two.

When he too had gone, the lord then created a third [son],
skilled in the path to liberation, the lord endowed with the name Svas.

He too, adopting that dharma, attained the very destination of those two.
In this way, all three sons of the great-souled Śambhu departed.

Taking those sons of his, those two departed to that exalted destination—
the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa and Kapila, the lord of ascetics.

At the very time they departed, O brāhmaṇa, Brahmā, at that very time,
again resorted to fiercer austerities, [intent upon] the supreme abode.

Yet the lord Brahmā was unable, performing austerities alone;
he then produced an auspicious wife from the half of his body.

The Grandfather indeed created sons equal to himself,
the universal lords of creatures from whom the worlds came forth:

First, by his austerity, the great-souled one [produced] a son, the lord of all,
merit combined everywhere, whom he created under the name Dharma;

Dakṣa, Marīci, Atri, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu,
Vasiṣṭha, Gautama, Bhṛgu, and the sage Aṅgiras.

These great seers are known to be exceedingly wonderful by their deeds;
they are thirteen initiators of virtues, the lineages of the great seers:

Aditi, Diti, Danu, Kālā, Anāyus, Siṃhikā, Khasā,
Prācī, Krodhā, Surasā, Vinatā, and Kadrū.

These were the offspring of Dakṣa, indeed twelve daughters, O king;
and the mighty asterisms of the Moon, twenty-seven in number.

Kaśyapa was the son of Marīci, fashioned indeed through austerity;
to him Dakṣa gave those twelve daughters with his consent,

and the seer likewise gave the asterisms to Soma—
all of them, beginning with Rohiṇī, which are sacred, O delight of the Kurus.

Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Saṃdhyā, and the greatly renowned Viśveśā,
and the goddess Sarasvatī were fashioned in ancient times by Brahmā.

These five foremost women were given to the best of gods, O king—
may you have good fortune—to Dharma, by Brahmā of observed deeds.

The wife of Brahmā, possessing half his form, who could assume any shape at will,
suddenly becoming Surabhi, approached Brahmā.

Then Brahmā, worshipped by the worlds, went to her in union,
knowing the purpose of creating the worlds, for the sake of cattle, O best of men.

And she gave birth to eleven vast sons designated as dharmas,
resembling the red twilight clouds, great ones of sharp splendor.

Weeping and running, they went to the Grandfather;
from weeping (rodana) and from running (dravaṇa), they are remembered as the Rudras.

Nirhṛti, Saṃdhya, and the third who was not born of a womb,
Mṛgavyādha, Kapardin, and he who is the great Viśveśvara,

the blessed Ahirbudhnya, Kapālin, and Piṅgala,
and the Senānī of great splendor—these are remembered as the eleven Rudras.

From that Surabhi alone were born the cows, and those who are gods, / and the goat, and the swan as well, O best of kings!

And the excellent medicinal herbs arose from Surabhi.
From Dharma, Lakṣmī bore Kāma, and Sādhyā bore the Sādhyas:

Bhava, Prabhava, Kṛśāśva, Suvaha,
Aruṇa, Varuṇa, Viśvāmitra, and the moving Dhruva,

Haviṣmant, Tanūja, and the two esteemed Vidhānas,
Vatsara, and Bhūti, the slayer of all Asuras.
The goddess, attendant upon Indra, gave birth to gods / having fair joints, immense splendour, and venerated by the Sādhyas' world:
Dhara, the first god, and Dhruva the imperishable, the second; / Viśvāvasu the third, and the lord Soma the fourth;
then Anurūpa, Māya, and next after him Yama; / seventh was Vāyu, and eighth Nirṛti.
This offspring of Dharma was born of Surabhi. / And the Viśvedevas are remembered as born to Dharma through Viśvā:
Dakṣa, the mighty-armed; Puṣkara, and Tamas; / Cākṣuṣa, then Atri; and likewise Bhadra and Mahoraga;
Viśvāntaka, Vasu, Bāla, and Nikumbha of great renown; / and Ruruda of exceedingly perfected power, radiant like the sun.
The mother of the gods bore the Viśvedevas as sons of Viśvā. / Marutvatī bore the gods who are the sons of Marutvān:
Agni, Cakṣus, Ravi, Jyotis, Sāvitrī, and Mitra; / Amara, Śaravṛṣṭi, Sukarṣa, and Mahattara;
Virāj, Rājā, Viśvāyu, and Sumati; / Aśvaga, Citraraśmi, and King Niṣadha;
moreover, Ātmavidhi, Cāritra, Pādamātraga, / Bṛhanta, Bṛhadrūpa, and Sanābhiga.
Marutvatī gave birth to offspring ending with Jyeṣṭha, the host of the Maruts. / Aditi bore to Kaśyapa the twelve Ādityas:
Indra, Viṣṇu, Bhaga, Tvaṣṭṛ, Varuṇa, Aṃśa, Aryaman, Ravi, / Pūṣan, Mitra the granter of boons, Dhātṛ, and Parjanya.
Thus these are the twelve Ādityas, the best of the heaven-dwellers. / To Āditya were born of Sarasvatī two excellent sons,
supreme in ascetic power, supreme in virtue, highly esteemed by heaven. / Danu gave birth to the Dānavas; Diti brought forth the Daityas;
Kālā brought forth the Kālakeyas, asuras and rākṣasas; / the sons of Anāyuṣā were mighty diseases;
Siṃhikā was the mother of planets; Muni the mother of gandharvas; / Prācī was the mother of apsarases, the most sacred of all, O descendant of Bharata;
Krodhā bore all the bhūtas, and Piśācā bore piśācas, O king; / and she gave birth to the hosts of yakṣas and rākṣasas, O lord of subjects.
Surabhi gave birth to four-footed creatures and these cattle. / And the primordial person, the lord Viṣṇu, Hari, through his illusion,
has been recounted to you in order, and praised by great ṛṣis. / And if a person constantly listens to this supreme Purāṇa, or recites it on sacred days,
attaining that world, freed from passion, he enjoys the fruits of heaven in the hereafter. / He who in four ways—by eye, mind, speech, and deed—
propitiates Kṛṣṇa, to him Kṛṣṇa is gracious. / A king obtains a kingdom, and an impoverished man supreme wealth;
one whose lifespan is depleted obtains life, and one desiring a son obtains progeny; / those seeking sacrifices obtain their desires, and various ascetic penances.
Whatever desire one may wish for, that he will receive from the Lord of the world. / If leaving aside everything, one recites this Pauṣkara
manifestation of Hari, O best of men, no misfortune shall befall him. / This manifestation of the great-souled one is indeed named Pauṣkara,
celebrated, O great king, following the teaching of Vyāsa and the Śruti. / Hear from me Viṣṇu's nature as Viṣṇu and his nature as Hari in the Kṛta age,
his nature as Vaikuṇṭha among the gods, and his nature as Kṛṣṇa among men; / for unfathomable is the course of the actions of that Lord.
Hear now as it is, O king, regarding the past and the future: / the unmanifest who resides in the manifest sign, who is this venerable Lord,
Nārāyaṇa, whose self is boundless, who is the source and dissolution of all— / having become this Nārāyaṇa, Hari became eternal:
Brahmā, Vāyu, Soma, Dharma, Indra, and Bṛhaspati. / And attaining sonship to Aditi, the unborn one, O delighter of the Kurus,
this all-pervading one became renowned as Viṣṇu, the younger brother of Indra. / The propitiation of that all-pervading one was the cause of Aditi's son,
for the destruction of the enemies of the gods—daityas, dānavas, and rakṣases. / Then at the beginning of the kalpa he created the gods, Brahmā, and the Prajāpatis;
he created mind-born sons there, the unexcelled lineages of Brahmā. / From those great-souled ones arose the supreme, eternal Brahman.
This deed of the wondrous Viṣṇu has been recounted; / hear now from me as I proclaim what is worthy of being proclaimed throughout the worlds.
When the slaying of Vṛtra had occurred, O Bhīṣma, in the ongoing Kṛta age, / there was a battle known in the three worlds, caused by Tāraka,
wherein all the dreadful Dānavas, hard to conquer in battle, / were slaying all the gods and asuras, along with yakṣas, uragas, and rākṣasas.
Being slaughtered and turning away, their weapons shattered in battle, / they went in mind to their protector, the divine Lord Nārāyaṇa.
In the meantime, clouds with the lustre of extinguished coals / covered the vault of the sky together with the sun, moon, and host of planets.
Accompanied by masses of fierce lightning and making terrible roars, / the seven winds blew, striking against one another with violent speed.
Carrying blazing waters, with thunderclaps, thunderbolts, fires, and winds, / with frightful cries and portents, the sky seemed as if being burned.
Thousands of meteors fell; sky-roamers also tumbled down; / and celestial aerial cars were falling and flying up.
Such fear as arises for the worlds at the end of the four ages / appeared in visible form amid those portents;
therefore everything was thrown into turmoil, and nothing could be discerned; / enveloped in floods of darkness, the ten directions did not shine.
A night personified entered, veiled in black clouds; / the sky did not shine, its sun overpowered, covered by dreadful darkness.
Tearing apart those masses of dense clouds and darkness with his arms, that Lord, / Hari, revealed his own divine dark form:
resembling a cloud and collyrium, with hair like clouds, / dark in splendour and form like a black mountain,
wearing radiant yellow garments, adorned with molten gold, / possessing a body like smoky darkness, like the fire at the end of an age arisen,
with round, doubly stout shoulders, his hair covered by a diadem, / he shone, embellished with weapons resembling gold,
gleaming like the rays of the moon and sun, high like a mountain peak, / bringing delight to Nandaka, his chest illuminated by the Kaustubha,
rising high with diverse fruits of power, bearing conch, discus, and mace, / the mountain that is Viṣṇu, forbearing in nature, marked with the Śrīvatsa, bow in hand,
yielding noble fruit to the thirty [gods], dear and beloved to celestial women, / dear to the minds of all worlds, captivating every creature,
with wide branches of illusion, having the lustre of a mass of clouds, / enriched by knowledge, ego, and pride, with the great elements as its offshoots,
covered with distinct leaves, in bloom with planets and constellations, / having the realm of Daityas as its massive trunk, giving light to the realm of mortals,
with a sound like that of an ocean, resting its neck upon Rasātala, / stretched out with the coils of the serpent kings, accompanied by birds and creatures,
abundant with the unshakeable fragrance of virtue, the great tree of all the worlds; / with the waters of unmanifest bliss, foamy with manifest ego,
with currents forming streams of the great elements, with bubbles of planets and asterisms, / pervaded by aerial chariots and conveyances, tumultuous with the grandeur of rain clouds.
Teeming with crowds of creatures as fish, filled with mountains as conch-shells, / whose whirlpools are the objects of the three qualities, swallowing all the worlds as a timiṅgila fish,
whose trees, creepers, and bushes are heroes, whose moss was shed by serpents, / having the twelve suns as its great islands, and the eleven Rudras as its cities,
endowed with the eight Vasus as its mountains, the great ocean of the waters of the three worlds, / with twilight and dusk as the water of its waves, beautified by the filled wind,
whose villages are the hosts of Daityas and Yakṣas, crowded with the hosts of Rākṣasas as large fish, / possessing the great prowess of the Grandfather, crowded with heavenly women as gems,
swarming with rivers as Śrī, Kīrti, Kānti, and Lakṣmī, / driven by the speed of the dissolution and creation in the great rains of the conjunction of Time,
whose far shore is the company of the virtuous—the great ocean that is Nārāyaṇa, / the God beyond the gods, the giver of boons, compassionate to his devotees,
the god who bestows grace, who brings about peace, the auspicious one— / on [a chariot] yoked with green-horsed chariot, adorned with the Garuda-standard,
having the moon and sun fashioned as its wheels, its interior surrounded by an expansive axle, / equipped with infinite rays, its chariot-pole difficult to look upon like Mount Meru,
having variegated flowers as the stars, charming with the planets and lunar mansions, / granting fearlessness in fears, in the sky, invincible to gods and Daityas—
standing in that chariot yoked with green horses, endowed with the luster of pearls, / consisting of the celestial world, they saw the god.
With folded hands, all those gods led by Indra, / raising shouts of victory, sought refuge with him who is the refuge.
Having heard their words, that Viṣṇu, the deity of the gods, / resolved in his mind upon the destruction of the Dānavas in great battle.
Stationed in the sky and having assumed his supreme form, Viṣṇu / spoke this word of solemn vow to all the deities:
“Attain peace! Good fortune to you! Do not fear, hosts of the gods! / All the Dānavas have been conquered by me; let the three worlds be taken back!”
Then, gratified by the speech of this true-vowed Viṣṇu, / the gods attained supreme joy, as if having drunk excellent nectar.
Then, darkness having been dispelled, the clouds disappeared; / auspicious breezes blew, and the ten quarters became clear.
The heavenly bodies, almost purely luminous, circumambulated the moon; / the planets did not wage war, and the seas became serene.
The pathways became dust-free, and the three worlds, heaven and the rest, [became peaceful]; / the rivers flowed in their proper course, and the ocean was not agitated as before.
The senses became tranquil within the inner selves of men; / the great sages, free from sorrow, recited the Vedas aloud.
In the sacrifices, the fire cooked the oblation auspiciously; / the people, in whom dharma had commenced anew, had joyful minds.
Having heard the words of Viṣṇu of true vow regarding the slaying of their enemies, / the Daiteyas and Dānavas then, hearing of danger from Viṣṇu's mouth,
made immense preparation for war and for victory. / Maya, however, [mounted] an imperishable [chariot] made of gold, measuring three nalvas across,
having four wheels, very expansive, well equipped with great weapons, / resounding with a net of small bells, covered with leopard-skin,
splendid with clusters of reins and adorned with golden latticework, / teeming with sculpted figures of wild animals and embellished with flocks of birds,
shining with celestial weapons and missiles, resounding like a raincloud, / having good axles, a noble and excellent chariot, with a spacious seat, resembling the sky,
filled with maces and iron clubs, like the embodied ocean, / with golden bracelets and armlets, its chariot-pole resembling the lunar orb,
equipped with pennants and banners, like Mount Mandara with the sun, / having the expansive frame of a lord of elephants, possessing the brilliance of filaments in some places,
yoked to a thousand bears, rumbling like a cloud showering a torrent of water, / radiant, moving through the sky, divine, a crusher of enemy chariots—
eager for battle, he mounted it, like the radiant sun upon Mount Meru. / Tāra, however, [mounted a chariot] a krośa in width and of the same dimension in length,
resembling a mountain-pole, like a heap of black collyrium, / its chariot-pole bound with masses of black iron and jewels,
emitting beams of darkness, like a thundering cloud, / armored with a great iron net equipped with latticed windows,
filled with iron clubs and hurling mallets, / with barbed darts, and with stretched-out snares and loose spikes,
adorned with terrifying javelins and with battle-axes, / raised up against enemies like a second Mount Mandara;
yoked to a thousand donkeys, he mounted that best of chariots. / Virocana, however, stood enraged, mace in hand,
at the front of his army, like a mountain with blazing peaks. / Yoked to a thousand horses, the Dānava Hayagrīva,
the mighty one, rode around the arrayed battle-formation of the Dānavas. / Vipracitti's son Śveta, adorned with white earrings,
drove his chariot, a crusher of the enemy's army, / drawing his great, taut bow measuring a thousand spans;
he stood at the front of the battle like a mountain with sprouting vegetation. / Khara, however, scattering from his eyes the water born of wrath,
with throbbing teeth, lips, and eyes, desired the combat. / The Dānava Tvaṣṭā, having mounted a vehicle drawn by eighteen horses,
stood facing the battle, resembling a divine battle-array. / Ariṣṭa, the son of Bali, superior and bearing weapons difficult to withstand,
stood facing the battle, causing the mountains to tremble. / Kiśora, however, driven by excessive joy, as if a youth,
stood in the midst of the Daityas like the sun in the midst of the planets. / Lamba, however, resembling a fresh cloud, adorned with hanging garments,
stationed in the Daitya battle-array, shone like the sun shrouded in mist. / Resembling the earth, then, with his teeth, lips, and eyes as weapons,
laughing, the cruel and mighty planet stood in the midst of the Daityas. / Others rode on horses there; others rode on furious lords of elephants;
others rode on lions and tigers, and others on boars and bears; / some rode on donkeys and camels, some had clouds as their vehicles;
and other Daityas were foot-soldiers, frightful and of deformed faces; / one-footed and footless ones danced, yearning for battle.
Many slapping their arms, and others roaring, / those foremost of Dānavas roared with the sounds of proud tigers.
Bearing rocks and mallets in hand, with terrible maces and clubs, / they threatened the deities with arms shaped like iron bars.
With barbed darts, swords, snares, javelins, elephant-goads, and sharp spears, / they sported with śataghnīs and hundred-edged mallets.
With sword-mountains and mountains, and with iron clubs raised as weapons, / joined with masses of clouds, the sky was covered on all sides.
Thus that Dānava army, furious with the intoxication of all creatures, / stood facing the deities like a rising army of clouds.
Dense with thousands of Daityas, like wind, fire, mountain, cloud, and water, / that army, teeming with floods of troops and raised up, shone forth as if maddened in its desire to fight.
You have heard the extent of the Daitya army, O delight of the Kurus; / hear now the extent of the army of the gods, pertaining to Viṣṇu.

1.41.m:
Pulastya said:
The Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, and the mighty Aśvins, / accompanied by their forces and followers, armed themselves in proper order.
In front, Puruhūta, the thousand-eyed guardian of the world, / the leader of all the gods, mounted his excellent elephant.
On his left side stood his chariot bearing the supreme bird as its emblem, / with wheels adorned like the sun, and ornamented with a golden parasol.
Followed by multitudes of gods, Gandharvas, and Yakṣas in their thousands, / he was extolled by radiant celestial sages dwelling in heaven.
Joined by clouds flashing with lightning and rainbows sparked by the thunderbolt, / which moved like winged mountains at will,
mounted upon which the Blessed One circles the entire world, / while brāhmaṇas standing at the threshold of the sacrifice sing at the offering of oblations.
As they set out for the celestial war and divine instruments resounded, / hundreds of hosts of apsarases danced before him together with Indra.
Shining like the sun with his banner of the serpent king, / yoked to a thousand horses swift as thought and wind,
that best of chariots shone splendidly, driven by Mātali, / just as Mount Meru is completely enveloped by the radiance of the sun.
Yama, lifting his staff and the club joined with death, / stood in the front line of the gods, showing himself to the Daityas.
Surrounded by the four oceans and by licking serpents, / wearing bracelets of conch and pearls, bearing a watery body,
brandishing the nooses of death, on horses resembling moonbeams / that appeared like wind-tossed water, displaying thousands of playful wonders,
with pale wind-fluttered garments and bracelets radiant as coral, / his supreme body dark as a jewel, his chest adorned with a necklace,
Varuṇa, holding his noose, stood in the center of the divine army, / longing for the moment of battle like an ocean overflowing its shores.
With an army of Yakṣas and Rākṣasas, and hosts of Guhyakas, / accompanied by the treasures Śaṅkha and Padma, the lord of treasures, the sovereign,
the glorious king of kings was seen, mace in hand, / fighting from an aerial car, Dhanada standing in the Puṣpaka.
That king of kings, the lord of Yakṣas who rides upon men, shone forth: / the thousand-eyed one held the eastern flank, and the king of ancestors the south;
Varuṇa held the western flank, and the one whose mount is man the north. / The four mighty world-guardians held the four flanks,
moving in their respective directions for that divine army. / The Sun, with his chariot drawn by seven horses, moving swift as the wind,
blazing with splendor, and shining with rays, / produced sunrise and sunset as he traveled along the edge of Meru.
With the wheel that is the gateway to heaven, illuminating the imperishable world through his ascetic heat, / endowed with a thousand rays and blazing with splendor,
the sun, having twelve forms, moved in the midst of the gods. / Soma, possessing cool rays, shone in his chariot drawn by white horses,
gladdening the world with beams filled with cool water, / followed by conjunctions with constellations, the cool-rayed lord of the twice-born.
his body marked by the hare's shadow, the destroyer of nocturnal darkness, / the lord of lights in the sky, who grants water, the imperishable master,
the receptacle of holy herbs and of nectar, / the supreme share of the universe, gentle and containing the essence of all,
the Dānavas saw, standing with ice as his weapon. / He who is the life-breath of all living beings, dividing into five within humans,
who moved in seven courses, upheld and created the three worlds, / whom they call the creator of fire, the source of all, the lord,
whose origin residing in the seven notes is proclaimed through hymns, / whom they call the moving element, whom they call the bodiless one,
whom they describe as moving through space, swift-traveling, and born of sound— / that Wind, the life of all beings, exalted by his own energy,
blew against the Daityas, terrifying them, accompanied by rain-clouds. / The Wind-god, together with gods, Gandharvas, and hosts of Vidyādharas,
played with bright rays like serpents sloughing their skins, / while the serpent lords cast forth sharp poison born of wrath;
clinging like arrows, with mouths wide open, they moved in the sky. / Mountains too, with rock peaks and trees of a hundred branches,
attended the hosts of the gods to strike the Dānava army. / That god who is Hṛṣīkeśa, lotus-navelled, taking three strides,
and the fire at the end of the cosmic age, the lord of the universe, / the source of all, the slayer of Madhu, consumer of oblations, present in the sacrifice,
the self of the elements earth, water, and sky, dark-complexioned, maker of peace, slayer of foes, / bearer of the discus and mace, ensured freedom from obstacle for the immortals and the rest.
With his left hand holding up the great mace that destroys all weapons, / which brought death to his enemies by its fatal form,
and with his other arms glowing brightly, the mighty lord whose banner bears the enemy of serpents / bore a network of weapons such as the bow Śārṅga and the rest.
Mounting the son of Kaśyapa, the bird who eats serpents, / who was resplendent with the lord of serpents held in his beak,
lofty like Mount Mandara when the churning for nectar began, / whose prowess was seen repeatedly in the clashes of gods and asuras,
marked by the great Indra with his thunderbolt for the sake of the nectar, / clothed in variegated plumage like a mountain rich in minerals,
with wide-spreading wrath, radiant like the moon, / clinging to the hoods of serpents, and shining with precious gems,
his wings of fair feathers spreading sportively in the sky / like two rain-clouds with rainbows at the end of a cosmic age,
adorned with blue, red, and yellow banners, / the glorious lord mounted the younger brother of Aruṇa in battle,
Suparṇa of golden hue, the best of birds that fly in the sky. / The hosts of the gods followed him, and the sages with concentrated minds
praised the bearer of the mace with hymns of supreme mantras. / That [army], closely joined with Vaiśravaṇa, led forward by the son of Vivasvat,
surrounded by the king of waters, resplendent with the king of gods, / having its roaring sound bound to the wind, its sacrificial fire blazing,
enveloped by the brilliance of the victorious, forbearing, and radiant Viṣṇu, / that mighty army advanced forcefully toward the battle.
“Hail to the gods!” Bṛhaspati declared; / “Hail to the Daityas!” Uśanas spoke.
A tumultuous conflict then arose between those two armies, / of the gods and asuras, both desiring victory over each other.
The Dānavas together with the deities, raising diverse weapons, / clashed in combat indeed like mountains with mountains.
That battle joined by the gods and asuras appeared wondrous indeed, / joined with righteousness and unrighteousness, with pride and with modesty.
Then, with swift horses and urged-on elephants, / and with warriors leaping into the sky on all sides with swords in hand,
with clubs hurled and arrows falling, / with bows stretched wide and terrible [weapons] brought down,
that battle became terrifying, crowded with gods and Dānavas, / causing terror to the world, resembling the destruction at the end of an age.
With iron bludgeons, clubs, and mountains hurled from their own hands, / the Dānavas in battle struck down the gods led by Indra.

Being slain by the powerful Dānavas who were proud of their victory,
the gods, with downcast faces, fell into great distress in the battle.

Crushed by weapons and spears, their heads broken by iron bludgeons,
their chests shattered by the sons of Diti, they bled profusely in the fight.

Tormented by networks of arrows and rendered powerless by shafts,
trapped within the Dānavas' sorcery, they were unable to move.

The army of the gods appeared as if paralyzed, looking lifeless,
its weapons rendered useless by the Asuras.

Cleaving with his thunderbolt those dreadful arrows loosed from the Daityas' bows,
Śakra of many eyes entered the terrible Daitya host.

Slaying all the foremost Daityas and their vast army,
he then turned it into darkness with a network of Tamas-weapons.

They did not recognize one another, nor did the vehicles of the Daityas,
enveloped by dreadful darkness through the splendour of Puruhūta.

Released from the nooses of magic, the striving foremost among the gods
struck down the heads of the Daitya multitudes that had become enveloped in darkness.

Overcome and senseless from the blue-black darkness,
those Dānavas instantly fell, like mountains with clipped wings.

There, the lord of the Daityas being overwhelmed, the interior became like darkness;
the bodily abode of the Dānavas turned as if into gloom.

Then Maya released a great sorcery that burned away that darkness,
producing the glare of a cosmic dissolution, created by Aurva's fire.

That [fire] devised by Maya consumed the illusion of Śakra,
and the Daityas, with bodies bright as the sun, immediately rose up in battle.

Encountering the fire of Aurva and burning, the denizens of heaven
resorted to the sphere of the moon, a watery pool of cool rays.

Burning with Aurva's fire, their minds distraught,
the tormented gods, seeking refuge, called out to the wielder of the thunderbolt.

As the army was scorched by magic and being slain by the Dānavas,
Varuṇa, urged by the king of the gods, spoke these words:

“Formerly, O Śakra, Urva, born of a Brahmarṣi and equal to Brahmā in virtues,
resplendent of old, performed severe tapas.

As he blazed with tapas like the sun, the immutable lord of the world,
multitudes of sages and the gods, along with celestial sages, approached him.
And Hiraṇyakaśipu, the Dānava and lord of the Dānavas, / made a request in ancient times to the sage of supreme splendour.
Those brahma-sages spoke words accompanied by dharma: / "Among the lineages of the sages, O lord, this family has its roots severed."

You are alone and childless, and no other exists for the lineage;
undertaking the vow of celibacy from youth, you merely pursue hardship.

Many brāhmaṇa lineages of cultivated sages
exist in a single body, isolated, without offspring.

When all are thus, there is no purpose for me with sons;
yet you are the foremost of ascetics, of splendour equal to Prajāpati.

Therefore, exert yourself for a lineage! Expand yourself through yourself!
Concentrate your powerful splendour, and create a second body!’

Thus addressed by the sages, the sage, struck to the heart,
reproached those multitudes of ṛṣis and spoke these words:

‘For the eternal dharma of sages was ordained of old
as solely the action of ṛṣis, subsisting on wild roots and fruits.

For a brāhmaṇa born of the source of the Veda and living according to the self,
well-practised brahmacarya can move even Brahmā.

Three are the livelihoods of men who dwell in the householder order;
and our livelihood is in the forest, dwelling in the forest-hermitage.

Those who subsist on water, those who feed on air, those who use teeth as mortars,
those who use stones as pestles, and those who perform the five-fire penance—

these, standing firm in tapas through vows very difficult to perform,
placing brahmacarya foremost, strive for the supreme state.

The brāhmaṇa status of a brāhmaṇa is ordained by brahmacarya;
so speak the people in the next world who know brahmacarya.

Dharma is established in brahmacarya; tapas is established in brahmacarya;
those brāhmaṇas who are established in brahmacarya abide in heaven.

There is no success without yoga; there is no fame without yoga;
there is no tapas in the world that is the root of fame higher than brahmacarya.

For one who restrains the senses and the collection of five elements
and concentrates upon brahmacarya, what higher tapas is there than this?

Wearing matted hair without yoga, performing vows without resolve,
and conducting oneself contrary to brahmacarya—these three are known as hypocrisy.

Where is a wife? Where is union? And where is the perversion of true disposition?
Was not this mental creation produced by Brahmā through the mind?

If you who have conquered yourselves possess the potency of tapas,
then produce mind-born sons through the rite of Prajāpati!

A womb fashioned by the mind should be impregnated by ascetics;
neither union with a wife nor seed is declared to be the vow of ascetics.

This which has been uttered here by you fearless and virtuous ones
is termed the destruction of dharma, highly approved [only] by the wicked.

Making this body of mind, my inner self blazing,
I shall produce a son, born of my own body, without union with a wife.

Thus my own self will generate a second self
according to the ordinance of Prajāpati, as if wishing to consume creatures.’

Varuṇa said:
‘Filled with tapas, Urva placed his thigh into the sacrificial fire
and churned the fire-kindling stick of his son's birth with a single blade of darbha grass.

Suddenly bursting forth from his thigh, an excellent fire arose;
desiring to consume the world, a son was born as fire.

Bursting forth from Urva's thigh, the fire named Aurva, like the god of death,
was born extremely wrathful, as if intending to burn the three worlds.

Being born, he spoke to his father in a plaintive voice:
“Hunger torments me, O father! Release me to devour the world!”

Flaring through the ten quarters with flames rising to heaven,
burning all creatures, he grew like the god of death.

At that moment Brahmā arrived before the sage Urva
and said, “Let your son be restrained! Have compassion on the world!

He will drink the waters, O brāhmaṇa; I will grant him excellent support.
Listen to these true words, O son, best among speakers!”

Aurva said:
“I am blessed, I am favoured, O lord, that you give this counsel
for the benefit of the supreme self, to me, an infant here.

When the dawn arrives, at the longed-for union,
with what offerings, O lord, will the son be satisfied and attain happiness?

Where would his dwelling be, and what would his food consist of?
The lord here will arrange what matches the power of this mighty one.”

There he shall abide constantly, drinking the watery oblation;
I assign that expanse of water as his abode, O brāhmaṇa.

Then at the end of the cosmic age, O little son, he and I
shall wander together here, putting an end to what is ancient.

At the time of destruction, this fire, feeding on water, made by me,
shall consume all creatures, along with gods, Asuras, and Rakṣases.”

Saying “So be it,” that fire, drawing in its circle of flames,
bowed to his father and lord, Urva, and entered into the mouth of the ocean.
Then Brahmā returned, and all those great sages, / knowing the power of Aurva's fire, went to their respective destinations.
Seeing that great wonder at that time, Hiraṇyakaśipu, / bowing down with all his limbs before Urva, spoke this word:
"O Lord, this wonder has taken place before the eyes of the worlds! / The Grandfather was thoroughly pleased with your austerity, O best of sages.
I, however, should be regarded as a servant of your son and of yourself, O you of great vows; / you are worthy of praise here on account of your deed.
Therefore, look upon me as arrived and devoted solely to your propitiation. / If I should perish, O best of sages, the defeat would be yours alone."
Urva said: / "I am blessed, I am favored, in that I am considered by you to be your guru. / You have no fear here, O you of virtuous vows, because of this austerity.
Take this very illusion created by my son, / fuel-less, made of fire, and difficult to touch even for fires.
Subject to you and your lineage for the restraint of enemies, / this will protect your own faction and burn the hostile faction."
Varuṇa said: / "This illusion is unbearable and hard even for the gods to approach, / fashioned formerly by Aurva, the fire who is the son of Urva.
However, once that Daitya is afflicted, it will undoubtedly become powerless, / for a curse was pronounced on it formerly by the very blazing power that created it.
If this is to be thwarted and the Lord made happy, / let the Night-maker, who is born of water, be given to me as a comrade, O Śakra.
Uniting with him and accompanied by aquatic creatures, / I shall destroy this illusion by your grace, no doubt."
Delighted, saying 'So be it,' Śakra, who causes the gods to thrive, / commanded Soma, whose weapon is cold, to advance for battle:
"Go, Soma, and become an ally of the noose-bearer, / for the destruction of the Asuras and the victory of the denizens of heaven.
You are considered his equal in power and the lord of the heavenly bodies; / the knowers of the Veda know that the fluids in all the worlds consist of you.
There is no one equal to you in this world, whose weapon is cold; / your waning and waxing are unmanifest in the ocean and in the sky.
You set time in motion through days and nights, bewitching the world; / your mark, made of the shadow of the earth, is the hare-shaped form on your lap.
The constellations born as your wives do not understand your illusory power, O Soma; / you stand above the path of the sun and above the heavenly bodies.
Dispelling darkness at once, you illuminate the entire universe; / the moon has cool rays and a frosty body, ruler of the heavenly bodies.
Moreover, he is the self of time and yoga, worthy of sacrifice, the chariot of sacrifice, imperishable, / the lord of herbs, the source of rites, the source of waters, having cool rays,
cool-rayed, the vessel of nectar, swift-moving, white-horsed; / you are beauty among beautiful forms, you are soma for soma-drinkers.
You are gentle to all beings, the destroyer of darkness, the king of lunar asterisms; / therefore, go, O mighty commander, along with Varuṇa who leads an army,
and pacify the Asuric illusion by which we are being burnt in battle." / Soma said: / "As you speak to me for the sake of battle, O king of gods and giver of boons,
here I shall shower cold that dispels the Daitya illusion; / see these [demons] scorched by my cold and wrapped in frost!"
Then, released by the Maker of Frost, showers of frost with nooses / enveloped those Daityas, like the wind enveloping masses of clouds.
Those two of great strength, Varuṇa and Indu, bearing nooses and cool rays, / struck the Dānavas with falls of frost and discharges of nooses.
Those two lords of water fighting with nooses and frost in battle / moved about in combat with waters like two agitated great oceans.
That entire great army of Dānavas was inundated by the two, / covered as if by heavy showers of cosmic-dissolution clouds.
Both Śaśāṅka and Varuṇa, the two lords of waters upraised, / pacified that illusion created by the king of the Daityas.
Burned by the net of cool rays and assailed by nooses in the battle, / the Daityas could not move, like headless mountains.
Smitten by the cool-rayed one, all those Daityas were brought down, / their entire bodies bathed in frost, like fires devoid of heat.
The splendid aerial chariots of those Daityas in the sky fell down; / variegated, they fell and flew up.
Seeing those Dānavas in the sky bound by the hand with nooses / and covered by cool rays, the sorcerer Dānava Maya

created on all sides a renowned mountainous illusion: / extended with networks of mountains, laughing with swords and broad blades, / resting upon heaps of peaks and trees, with forests crowded with caves,
crowded with herds of lions and tigers, with roaring divine troop-commanders, / crowded with herds of phantom-deer, its trees shaken by the wind,
created by his own son, shrieking in the sky and moving at will.
With clashing sounds of swords, showers of rocks, and falling trees, / it struck down the hosts of gods and revived those Dānavas.
Then, the lunar and Vāruṇa illusions vanished; / the earth became dreadful to traverse, as if with mountains.
Not a single god, obstructed by masses of trees, could be seen; / with bows smashed and turbid with broken weapons,
the army of the gods was reduced to inaction, except for the bearer of the mace; / for he, the glorious Lord engaged in the battle, did not waver.
Out of patience, the master of the universe, bearer of the mace, did not become angry; / knowing the proper time and resembling a dark cloud of doom, he looked out for the right moment in battle,
for Hari was wishing at that time to witness the clash between gods and Asuras. / Then, commanded by the Lord, Fire and Wind in the battle,
prompted by Viṣṇu's command, dispersed the illusion. / With their speed unleashed, both aroused in the great battle,
that mountainous illusion was burnt, turned to ash, and destroyed. / That wind combined with fire, and that fire agitated by the wind,
burnt the army of the Daityas, raging as if at the ends of cosmic ages; / the wind rushed ahead there, and the fire followed the wind.
Fire and Wind roamed sporting within the army of the Dānavas; / as beings were turned to ashes, falling down and flying up,
and the aerial chariots of the Dānavas fell down on all sides, / tossed by the masses of wind, the Fire having performed its work,
when the destruction of the illusion had commenced and the bearer of the mace was being praised, / when the Daityas were reduced to inaction and the three worlds freed from bondage,
when the gods were joyful and uttering 'Well done! Well done!', / upon the victory of the Thousand-eyed One and the defeat of the Daityas,
when all directions were pure and the expansion of dharma proceeded, / when the path of the moon was unveiled and the sun stood in its own station,
when beings were established in right conduct and men possessed good character, / when death's bond remained intact and oblations were offered into the fire,
when gods shone with sacrifices and indicated the path to heaven, / when all the world-protectors remained firm in maintaining the quarters,
when the presence of those accomplished in austerity was ensured and the absence of evil-doers obtained, / when the gods' faction rejoiced and the Daityas' faction despaired,
when dharma stood on three legs and adharma on only one leg, / when the great gate was opened wide and the righteous path was practiced,
when the worlds were engaged in dharma and the hermitage stages functioned, / when kings engaged in protecting their subjects and shone brightly,
when the worlds were pacified and the darkness of the Dānavas subsided, / and when the deed of war was accomplished by Fire and Wind—
Filled with him, of spotless vision, having accomplished victory through both of them, / hearing the intense and great terror of the Daityas caused by wind and fire,
the Dānava known as Kālanemi appeared, / wearing a diadem shaped like the sun, with jingling ornaments and armlets,
resembling Mount Mandara, clad in gold, / towering with a hundred weapons, having a hundred arms and a hundred faces,
having a hundred heads, standing glorious like a mountain with a hundred peaks, / grown huge like a summer fire in a thicket of dry grass,
with smoke-colored hair, tawny beard, prominent teeth, and a gaping mouth, / holding a vast body that extended through the mid-region between the three worlds,
balancing the sky with his arms, kicking down the mountains with his feet, / driving forth with his breaths from the mouth rain-bearing clouds,
with broad, blood-red eyes turned sideways, possessing the towering splendor of Mount Mandara, / advancing in the battle as though wishing to burn up all the hosts of gods,
threatening the hosts of gods, covering the ten directions, / like Death himself seen risen, bristling at the time of cosmic dissolution.
With an exalted, excellent palm with broad finger-joints, / laden with dangling ornaments, slightly agitated in its movements,
with his raised, shapely right forehand, / he spoke to the Dānavas struck down by the gods, saying, "Stand firm!"
At that Kālanemi, the wheel of death for his foes in battle, / all the gods gazed with eyes trembling in terror.
The beings watched that Kālanemi swallowing [everything], / striding forth like a second Nārāyaṇa who took three strides.
Having attained immense height again, his garments stirred by the wind, / the Asura stepped forward to fight, terrifying all the deities.
Having encountered the lord of the gods, turning around locked in combat, / the Daitya Kālanemi shone like Mount Mandara entwined by Viṣṇu.
Then all the gods, led by Śakra, trembled / upon seeing Kālanemi advancing like another Time of Death.
Desiring to please the Dānavas, the great Asura Kālanemi / grew mightily in majesty, like a rain cloud at the end of summer.
Seeing him standing within the three worlds, those lords of the Dānavas / rose up untired, as though they had drunk the supreme nectar.
Free from fear and terror, led by Maya and Tāra, / always appearing victorious in the Tārakāmaya war,
the Dānavas eager for battle shone on the field of combat; / repeating their spells and running along the array,
they felt great joy at the sight of the Dānava Kālanemi. / Those leaders who stood in front of the battle for Maya,
casting aside all fear, stepped forward delighted to fight: / Maya, Tāra, Varāha, and the Dānava Hayagrīva,
Vipracitti’s son Śveta, both Khara and Lamba, / Ariṣṭa, the son of Bali, and the one named Kiśora,
Svarbhānu resembling an immortal, and the great Asura Cakrayodhin; / all of them were masters of weapons, all firmly established in asceticism.
The skilled Dānavas went to the haughty Kālanemi; / they, with very heavy maces, with discs and axes,
with pestles like Death, with throwable clubs, / with stones resembling missiles, and with dreadful rocks,
with paṭṭiśa halberds, bhindi-pālas, and iron bars of the finest steel, / with deadly, heavy śataghnīs,
with yokes, with projectiles released from engines, with plows striking fiercely, / with outstretched arms, and with nooses, iron bars, and the like,
with gliding arrows darting forth like flickering serpents' mouths, / with striking thunderbolts, and with blazing javelins,
with unsheathed, sharp swords, with whetted, stainless spears, / blazing Daityas who had seized their bows,
then, having placed Kālanemi at their head in battle, / that army of the Daityas, with its radiant, supreme weapons, shone brightly.
Like a forest grove at the onset of rain whose every limb is drawn tight, / the army of the deities, guarded by Śakra, also rejoiced.
Endowed with the cool and hot radiances of the moon and the sun, / swift as the wind, serene, flagged with hosts of stars,
garbed in clouds, smiling with planets and asterisms, / guarded by Yama, Indra, Dhanada, and the wise Varuṇa,
resplendent with blazing fire and wind, devoted to Nārāyaṇa, / that great, blazing army, resembling the surge of the ocean,
shone formidable with weapons, graced by Yakṣas and Gandharvas. / Then indeed occurred the clash of those two armies,
as though it were the meeting of heaven and earth at the end of an age; / dreadful was that fight, crowded with gods and Dānavas.
Intent on endurance and prowess, giving vent to pride and discipline, / the gods and the Asuras rushed forth from their two terrible hosts,
like clouds raging from the eastern and western oceans. / Thrilled with those two armies, the gods and Dānavas moved about
like flowering trees from two mountain forests. / Likewise, they struck kettledrums and blew conches many times,
filling the cosmic egg, the earth, and the quarters of the sky. / The sounds of bowstrings hitting palm-guards, the twang of bows,
and the roar of dundubhi drums drowned out the Daityas' voices. / They rushed against one another, tormenting each other.
Eager to fight, they broke limbs with their arms in wrestling; / the terrible thunderbolts of the gods, iron bars as supreme weapons,
swords, and heavy maces were discharged by the Dānavas in battle. / Their bodies shattered by the falls of maces and cut to pieces by arrows,
some fell down violently, while others struck again. / Then, with chariots, horses, flying cars, and foot soldiers,
they clashed furiously in battle out of mutual rage, / whirling around in the fight with lips bitten in anger.
Chariot-warriors fought with chariot-warriors, and infantry with infantry; / the tumult of those chariots, noisy and carrying clamor,
made the sky resound, as if in the month of Nabhasya with the roars of clouds. / Some smashed chariots, while others were crushed by chariots;
other chariots, trapped in the press, could not move. / Raising each other up with their arms in the midst of battle, the armored warriors,
roaring loudly, powerful, struck there with sword and shield. / Others, pierced by divine missiles, vomited blood when slain in combat.
Resembling clouds gathered together pouring down water, / the dark storm of battle shone with the mutual shower of arrows.
Meanwhile, that enraged Dānava Kālanemi / swelled like a cloud being filled by surges of the ocean.
From his limbs resembling mountain peaks, clouds descended, / crowned with flashes of lightning and raining blazing thunderbolts.
As he breathed in fury, raining sweat with knitted brows, / spreading flames accompanied by sparks of fire issued from his mouth.
Across and upward into the sky his arms grew, / like five-headed serpents emerging from a mountain.
With many kinds of weapon-nets, bows, and iron bars, / he covered the celestial sky as if with towering mountains.
With garments stirred by the wind, he stood, eager for battle, / like Mount Meru itself, its crags touched by twilight's glow.
With mountain peaks and towering trees violently shaken by the force of his thighs, / he brought down hosts of gods as if striking great mountains with the thunderbolt.
And with swords in hand, their hair cut and disheveled by his arms, / the gods, struck by Kālanemi, were unable to move in battle.
Some were struck down with fists, and others were cleaved in two: / Yakṣas, Gandharvas, and birds, along with great serpents and Kinnaras.
Terrified by Kālanemi, they fell on the battlefield; / though they tried, those bewildered beings could make no effort.
By him Śakra of a thousand eyes was immobilized by bindings of arrows; / rendered powerless in battle, he indeed could not stir.
Looking like a cloud without water, bearing the splendor of an ocean drained of water, / deprived of his noose, Varuṇa was rendered inactive in combat by him.
In battle, Vaiśravaṇa was surrounded by him whose form was Time; / weeping, that lord of world-guardians, the giver of wealth, was forced to abandon his function.
Yama, who takes all away, weaponed with death in battle, / abandoned his southern station out of fear of him and entered his own quarter.
Having driven away the world-guardians and seized their functions, / he then divided his own body into four parts across all directions.
Ascending to the divine path of the asterisms shown by Svarbhānu, / he seized the splendor of the Moon and what was his great domain.
He caused the Sun, the hot-rayed one, who is the doorway to dharma, to tremble; / he seized his command, his realm, and his duty of making day.
Having conquered Fire, the mouth of the gods, he made him dwell in his own mouth; / and having conquered the Wind with his speed, he brought him under his own control.
Gathering by force all the rivers from the ocean, / he directed them favorably, and the seas became his very body.
Bringing under his own sway the waters born in heaven and those born on earth, / he enveloped the world well guarded by mountains.
He shone like the Self-born himself, the great lord of primeval beings; / the Daitya, embodying all the worlds, brought terror to all the worlds.
Having the single body of the world-guardians, soul of the moon, sun, and planets, / sprung from fire and wind, the Dānava shone in battle.
Established in the place of the Supreme Being, resembling the origin of the worlds, / hosts of Daityas praised him as gods praise the Grandfather.
Five did not attend upon him on account of his contrary conduct: / the Veda, dharma, patience, truth, and Śrī, who relies on Nārāyaṇa.
Furious at the non-appearance of these, the lord of Dānavas, / seeking out the abode of Viṣṇu, went where the deity was.
He saw [him] mounted on Suparṇa, holding conch, discus, and mace, / whirling his splendid mace for the destruction of the Dānavas,
resembling a raincloud full of water, wearing garments like lightning, / mounted upon the sky-roaming bird, offspring of Kaśyapa, rich in golden wings.
Seeing unshakeable Viṣṇu standing in the sky as if poised to destroy wicked Daityas, / the Dānava spoke with an agitated mind:
"This is that enemy of ours, the destroyer of our forefathers' lives, / and also of Madhu and Kaiṭabha who dwelt in the ocean.
This is that enemy of ours, said indeed to be unequaled, / by whom many Dānavas were slain through countless battles.
This is that pitiless one in the world, shameless before women and children, / by whom the parting of the hair of the Dānava women was unadorned.
This is that Viṣṇu to the gods, and Vaikuṇṭha to the celestials, / Ananta among serpents, and the Self-born among self-born beings.
This is that protector of the gods who is dragged down by us; / having incurred his wrath, Hiraṇyakaśipu was slain.
Relying on his shadow, the gods, stationed at the mouth of sacrifice, / partake of the clarified butter offered in three ways by the great sages.
This is the cause of destruction for all the foes of the immortals; / entered into his discus, our clans perished in battle.
This is he who, in battles, has reportedly surrendered his life for the sake of the gods; / that lord hurls at his foes a discus endowed with fiery splendor.
This is death to the Daityas; when I am stationed here as death personified, / Keśava shall reap the fruit of his past deeds.
Fortunately, this Viṣṇu has now arrived before my eyes; / crushed in battle by many blows, he shall perish at my hands alone.
Today in combat I shall gladly pay the debt to my ancestors, / having slain this Nārāyaṇa who strikes terror into the Dānavas.
Quickly shall I slay the hosts of immortals in battle; / even when born in other species, he torments the Dānavas in combat.
In ancient times, becoming Ananta, famed as Padmanābha, / he slew both Madhu and Kaiṭabha in the terrible single ocean.
Making his body two-fold, half-lion and half-man, / he alone of old slew my father, Hiraṇyakaśipu.
Aditi, kindling-stick of the gods, bore him as an auspicious embryo; / he alone seized the three worlds while striding with three strides.
Now again, when this battle concerning Tāraka has arrived, / encountering me, he along with the gods shall perish!"
Having thus spoken manifold [abuses] against Nārāyaṇa in battle, / with unfitting words he sought only war.
Assailed by the lord of Asuras, the bearer of the mace did not grow angry; / with great strength born of forbearance, he smiled and said this:
"Small is the strength born of arrogance, O Daitya; enduring is the strength born of non-anger. / You are destroyed by vices born of arrogance, who talk without patience.
You are vile in my view; fie upon this strength of your words! / Who are the men where women roar?
I see you, O Daitya, treading the path of your ancestors; / who can have well-being after abandoning Prajāpati, the ordained boundary?
Today I shall destroy you, the obstructor of divine functions, / and I will establish the gods each in their own stations."
While the bearer of the Śrīvatsa was thus speaking in battle, / the Dānava laughed in fury and armed his hands with a discus.
Raising a hundred arms bearing hosts of all kinds of weapons in battle, / with eyes doubly red from wrath, he struck at Viṣṇu's chest.
The Dānavas too, headed by Maya and Tāra, / with upraised weapons and swords rushed at Viṣṇu in battle.
Struck by those exceedingly strong Daityas with raised weapons of all kinds, / he did not waver in the battle, like a mountain being shaken.
Engaged with Suparṇa, the great Asura Kālanemi, / raising with all his might a huge mace with his arms,
terrible and blazing, hurled it in fury upon Garuḍa; / at that deed of the Daitya, Viṣṇu was filled with wonder.
Then that mace was hurled by him onto the head of Suparṇa; / seeing Suparṇa distressed and his own body wounded,
Vaikuṇṭha, his eyes blood-red with wrath, seized his discus; / and with Suparṇa the all-pervading lord grew swiftly in size.
His arms expanded, pervading the ten directions / and the intermediate spaces, filling both the sky and the earth.
He grew again by his splendor, as if wishing to stride through the worlds; / as he grew in the vault of the sky for the conquest of the leaders of Asuras,
the sages along with the Gandharvas praised Madhusūdana, / scraping the firmament with his diadem and with his radiant head,
stepping over the earth with his two feet, covering the quarters with his arms, / resembling a thousand suns, thousand-spoked, the destroyer of foes.
resembling a blazing fire, terrible, Sudarśana to behold, / edged with gold dust, with a diamond-hard nave, causing terror,
besprinkled with the fat, bones, marrow, and blood sprung from Dānavas, / an unequalled weapon whose circular rim was like a razor,
hung with garlands of flowered chaplets, moving at will, changing form at will, / created by the Self-born himself, striking fear into all enemies.
Filled with rage, he held it, ever proud in battle, / by whose hurling the worlds together with the stationary and moving are bewildered,
and carrion-eating beings find satisfaction in the great fight. / Raising the disc in battle, with matchless deeds, equal to the sun in splendor,
the wielder of the mace, ablaze with anger, destroying the Dānava's / splendor with his own brilliance,
severed with it the arms of Kālanemi in combat, / and that terrible hundred of faces, shouting violent laughter with fire and powder,
of that Daitya, Hari forcibly crushed with his disc. / With arms severed, headless, the Dānava did not tremble;
he stood as a headless trunk in battle, like a branchless tree. / Spreading his two great wings, matching the speed of the wind,
Garuḍa struck Kālanemi on the chest. / That armless body of his, spinning as it faced the sky,
fell down, abandoning the heavens, shaking the surface of the earth. / When that Daitya had fallen, the gods together with the hosts of ṛṣis,
having assembled, worshipped Vaikuṇṭha, crying, 'Well done! Well done!' / But the other Daityas whose prowess was seen in battle,
they were all surrounded by his arms and were unable to move in the fight. / He seized some by the hair, and crushed others by the neck;
he cut off the face of one, and seized another by the waist. / Consumed by the mace and disc, bereft of strength and devoid of life,
all their limbs broken, they fell from the sky onto the surface of the earth. / When all those Daityas were slain, the Supreme Person,
the wielder of the mace, having accomplished his task and done what pleased Śakra / in that crushing encounter, in that battle over Tārakā,
Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, quickly went to that place / together with all the brahmarṣis and the hosts of Gandharvas and Apsarases.
The god, worshipping Hari, the god of gods, spoke these words: / 'A great deed has been done, O God; the thorn of the gods has been removed,
and by the destruction of the Daityas, we too are fully satisfied. / As for this great Asura Kālanemi who was slain by you, O Viṣṇu,
Indeed, apart from you there is no ruler of him in this world. / Overpowering the gods and the worlds with all that moves and is still,
making slaughter of the sages, he roars even against me! / Therefore, by this deed of yours I am well pleased.
that this Kālanemi, who was like Death itself, was felled by you. / Therefore, come—blessings be upon you—let us go to the supreme heaven.
The brahmarṣis abiding there, having gathered in assembly, await you. / And what boon shall I give you, O best of boon-granting lords?
When the gods are established in their own places, you are the giver of boons to them. / This thriving three-world has been delivered, its thorn destroyed,
in this very battle, O Viṣṇu, for the sake of the high-souled Śakra.' / Being addressed in this way by the blessed Brahmā, the imperishable Hari
spoke in auspicious speech to all the gods headed by Śakra. / Viṣṇu said: / 'Let all the thirty gods who are gathered here listen:
Accompanied by Garuḍa, placing Puraṃdara at the head, / we all have slain the [demons] led by Kālanemi in combat—
Dānavas endowed with valor, greater even than Śakra. / In this great battle, only two have escaped:
Virocana, the son of Diti, and the mighty Svarbhānu. / Let Śakra resort to his own quarter, and Varuṇa to his quarter;
Let Yama protect the southern quarter, and the lord of wealth the northern quarter! / And let the moon always go to conjunction with the constellations!
let the sun resort to the beginning of the seasons along with his courses; / let the shares of clarified butter be offered, honored by the priests in the hall;
let fires be fed by the brāhmaṇas with rituals seen in the Veda; / and let the gods be pleased with food-offerings and oblations, the great ṛṣis with self-study of the Veda,
and the ancestors with ancestral rites, according to their pleasure. / Let the wind move along its path; let the fire blaze threefold;
let the three castes satisfy the three worlds with their inborn virtues; / let sacrifices be undertaken by the twice-born with rites of consecration;
let sacrificial gifts be distributed severally by the sacrificers; / let the sun [nourish] the rays, the moon the juices, and the wind the life-breaths among living creatures;
gratifying them, let these go about their gentle functions. / Let the rivers, mothers of the three worlds, originating from Mahendra and Malaya,
duly proceed in order to the ocean; / let fear of the Daityas be cast aside, and do you deities attain peace.
May it be well with you; I shall go to the eternal realm of Brahmā. / In one's own house, or in heaven, or especially in battle,
one must not walk about trusting [them], for the Dānavas are ever base; / they strike at vulnerable points; there is no steady conduct in them.
You who are gentle by nature, let your mind be fixed on uprightness.' / Having spoken thus to the hosts of gods, Viṣṇu of true prowess,
the glorious one, the blessed lord, creating great joy among the gods, / went together with Brahmā to the realm of Brahmā.
This wondrous event took place in the battle over Tārakā / between the Dānavas and Viṣṇu, about which you ask me.

1.42.m: Bhīṣma said: / 'The lotus-born creation has been heard, O brāhmaṇa, as expounded by you in detail; / in brief, the greatness of Bhava and the origin of Guha,
I wish to hear from you, O brāhmaṇa, as it occurred and what was done. / And how did Tāraka become such a more powerful Dānava?
How was that great Asura destroyed by Kārttikeya, O brāhmaṇa? / How were the sages sent by Rudra to Mount Mandara?
How was Umā obtained there by Rudra, the supreme lord? / Tell me all of this as it happened, O great sage.'
Pulastya said: / 'Formerly, the auspicious Diti, kindling-stick of the Daityas, was told by Kaśyapa: / "O goddess, you will have a son with limbs made of the essence of the diamond,
a son named Vajrāṅga, devoted to righteousness." / And that goddess, having obtained the boon, gave birth to him who was hard to pierce even by the thunderbolt.
As soon as he was born, he mastered the meaning of all treatises. / He spoke to his mother with devotion: "Mother, what shall I do?"
Then Diti, delighted, said to that lord of Daityas: / "Many sons of mine were slain by the Thousand-Eyed one, my child.
To take vengeance for them, go and slay Śakra." / Saying "So be it!" to her, he went by force to heaven.
Then, binding the Thousand-Eyed one with a noose of unfailing power, / he came to the presence of his mother, like a hunter with a small deer.'

Meanwhile, Brahmā and Kaśyapa of great austerities
arrived where the mother and son stood fearless.

Having seen the two of them, Brahmā and Kaśyapa spoke thus:
"Release him, son, the king of gods! What purpose is served by him?

For an honored man, son, humiliation is said to be death.
He who is released from your hands at our word is already dead!

An enemy of his foes who is freed in battle out of respect for another
is indeed dead day after day, even while living!"

Hearing this, Vajrāṅga bowed and said:
"I have no business with him; I only carried out my mother’s command.

You are indeed the lord of gods and asuras, venerable and our great-grandfather.
I shall do your bidding, O god; Śatakratu is released.

My delight is in austerity, O god; may it be free of obstacles for me
by your grace, O Blessed One!" Having spoken thus, he fell silent.

When that Daitya had become quiet, the Grandfather spoke this:
Brahmā said:
"Perform austerity, fallen into no [misfortune], abiding by our decree.

Indeed, by this purity of mind the fruit of birth is fully attained."
Having spoken thus, the Lotus-born created a wide-eyed maiden.

The god, the Lotus-born, gave her to him for a wife;
and having given her the name Varāṅgī, the Grandfather departed.

Vajrāṅga, too, went with her to the forest for austerity.
With arms raised up, that king of Daityas practiced for a thousand years,

a time, lotus-leaf-eyed, of pure intellect and great austerity;
and for that much time with head hung down, and for that much time standing amid five fires;

fasting, of terrible asceticism, he became a mass of austerity.
Then he made his dwelling within the water for a thousand years.

When he had entered within the water, his wife of great vows,
abiding in silence, remained on the bank of that very lake.

Fasting, she of great luster entered upon terrible austerity.
While she was engaged in austerity, Indra produced terrifying frights.

Taking the form of a monkey, the mighty one went to that great hermitage,
and dragged away her grass-mat, perfume, and basket for worship.

Then, in the form of a lion, he terrified the lovely woman;
and then, in the form of a serpent, he bit her two feet.

Yet through the power of her austerity, she did not meet destruction.
Tormenting her with numerous terrors, Pākaśāsana

did not cease at all. Then Vajrāṅga’s queen,
thinking the mountain to be wicked, prepared to pronounce a curse.

Seeing her intent on a curse, the mountain took human form,
and with frightened eyes spoke to her of lovely hips, Varāṅgī:

The mountain said:
"I am not wicked, O woman of great vows! I am to be sought for refuge by all living beings.
It is this enraged Pākaśāsana who does what is displeasing to you."

Meanwhile, the span of a thousand years elapsed.
Knowing that time, the Blessed One, the Lotus-born,

approached the reservoir pleased and spoke to Vajrāṅga:
Brahmā said:
"I grant all your desires; arise, O son of Diti!"

Thus addressed, that king of Daityas, a treasury of austerities, arose
and with folded hands spoke these words to the Grandfather of all the worlds:

Saying "So be it," the god departed to his own abode.
When his austerity was concluded, Vajrāṅga of firm self-restraint,

wishing to join his wife, did not see her in his hermitage.
Afflicted by hunger, he entered the dense thicket of the mountain

to gather fruits and roots, and there he saw
his own beloved, weeping and wretched, her face hidden behind a tree.

Seeing her, the Daitya then spoke, comforting her:
Vajrāṅga said:
"By whom was an offense committed against you, auspicious one, wishing to go to the realm of Yama?

Or what desire should I grant? Speak quickly, proud woman!"
Varāṅgī said:
"I have been frightened, thrown down, struck, and harassed

repeatedly by the fierce king of gods, as though I had no protector!
Seeing no end to my sorrow, I have resolved to give up my life.

Give me a son, Tāraka, [to save me] from this great ocean of grief!"
Addressed thus, that king of Daityas, his eyes agitated with anger,

though capable of retaliating against the king of the gods, the great Asura,
mighty in strength, resolved only to perform austerity again.

Knowing his even fiercer resolution, Brahmā
came with haste to where the son of Diti was.

Brahmā said:
"Why, son, are you again intent upon undertaking a vow?
I shall give you again the desired son by my power."

'Give me a son, Tāraka!' You are pleased with me, O Grandfather."
Brahmā said:
"Enough of your austerity, O hero! Do not enter into insurmountable affliction.

Your son named Tāraka shall indeed be of great strength,
one who unbinds the braided hair of the wives of the gods!"
Thus addressed, the lord of the Daityas bowed down to the great-grandfather; / having gone, he brought joy to that chief queen who was extremely emaciated.

Having attained their desire, the husband and wife then went to their hermitage.
Then Varāṅgī, of excellent complexion, conceived a fetus;

she bore it in her womb for a full thousand years.
Then, at the end of the thousand years, that Varāṅgī gave birth.

As that Daitya, who brought fear to the world, was being born,
the whole earth shook and the great oceans rose up.

The mountains also trembled, and frightful winds blew;
the best sages recited their prayers, and even beasts of prey and wild animals cried out.

The moon and sun lost their luster, and the directions were veiled in mist.
When that great Asura was born, all the great Asuras

and the Asura women came there overjoyed;
they sang filled with joy, and the hosts of Apsarases danced.

When that great festival of the Dānavas took place, O you of great luster,
the gods along with Indra became dejected at heart.

Seeing her son, Varāṅgī was then filled with joy,
and the king of Daityas held him in high esteem, born then by her.

As soon as he was born, that king of Daityas, Tāraka of fierce prowess,
was consecrated by the foremost Asuras, Kujambha, Mahiṣa, and others,

in the great sovereignty over all Asuras, capable of weighing the earth.
Having attained that great sovereignty, Tāraka, O best of kings,

the foremost Dānava spoke these reasonable words:
Tāraka said:
"Listen to my words, all you Asuras of great strength!

The gods are destroyers of the lineage of all Dānavas;
by our innate duty, an imperishable hostility has sprung up between us.

We shall perform austerity to subdue the gods,
relying on the strength of our own arms, all of us, without doubt!"

Hearing that, having agreed, he went to the Pāriyātra mountain.
Fasting, practicing the five fires, eating leaves, and subsisting on water,

he performed these austerities for a hundred years each in this manner.
When his body was thus emaciated and had become a mass of austerity,

Brahmā approached and said to the king of Daityas: "Choose a boon, O man of good vows!"
He chose: "May I have no death from any living beings!"
Then Brahmā said to him: "Death is certain for embodied beings. / Choose, therefore, your death from whatever source you do not fear."
Then the lord of the Daityas considered, and, deluded by pride, / the great Asura chose death from an infant seven days old.
Saying "Om!", Brahmā departed, and the Daitya went to his own home. / Then he said to his ministers: "Quickly assemble my army!"
"If you wish to do what pleases me, the foremost gods must be captured; / when they are captured, O Asuras, matchless joy will arise in me."
Hearing Tāraka's words, the Dānava named Grasana, / commander of the Daitya king's army, made that force ready.
Quickly beating the deep drum and summoning the Daityas, / [there gathered] Daitya lords of ten crores [of troops], Daityas of fierce prowess.
Foremost among them was Jambha, and next to him the Asura Kujambha, / Mahiṣa, Kuñjara, Megha, Kālanemi, and Nimi,
Manthana, Jambhaka, and Śumbha: ten leaders, lords among Daityas; / and hundreds of others were there, capable of weighing down the earth.
Drawn by a thousand Garuḍas, adorned with eight wheels, / furnished with a carriage-pole and side-frames, four yojanas wide—
such was the chariot of Tāraka; while yoked with tigers, lions, donkeys, and horses / were the chariots of Grasana, Jambhaka, Kujambha, and Kumbhin.
Megha's chariot was yoked with panthers, Kālanemi's with kūṣmāṇḍa demons; / and Nimi had a great elephant resembling a mountain, with four tusks.
Mounted on a horse a hundred cubits high was the Daitya king named Manthana; / Jambhaka, of great strength, rode a camel resembling the lord of mountains;
Śumbha mounted a ram, and the others likewise had varied mounts, / fierce, clad in varied armor, adorned with earrings and turbans.
Terrible in form became that army of the Daitya lion, / crowded with rutting and infuriated elephants, horses, and chariots.
Having many foot soldiers and banners, it set out for battle with the gods. / Meanwhile, Vāyu, the gods' messenger in the Asuras' abode,
seeing that Dānava army, went to report to Indra. / Having arrived at the divine assembly of the great-souled Mahendra,
he declared among the gods that urgent matter at hand. / Hearing that, the king of gods, with eyes closed,
mighty-armed, addressed this timely word to Bṛhaspati. / Indra said: / "This clash of the gods with the Dānavas is imminent.
Tell me what must be done here, supported by policy and statecraft." / Having heard this word of Mahendra, the lord of speech,
Thus spoke the fortunate Bṛhaspati of noble intellect. / Bṛhaspati said: / "Policy begins with conciliation, as has been heard; the fourfold army with banners..."
For those desiring victory, O best of the gods, this is the eternal rule: / conciliation, dissension, bribery, and force are the four limbs.
Greedy beings do not fall within the scope of conciliation; those of common purpose cannot be divided; / and bribery cannot bring success against those who take by sheer force.
The only means here is force, if you approve." / Thus addressed, the thousand-eyed [Indra] said, "So it is,"
and having considered what was to be done, spoke in the assembly of the immortals. / Indra said: / "Listen with attention to my words, O dwellers of heaven!
You are enjoyers of sacrifices, of divine nature, with your retinues, / ever established in your own glory, devoted to protecting the world.
Let preparations for battle be made; let my army be mobilized! / Let weapons be brought, and let the deities of weapons be worshipped!
Yoke my mounts and flying chariots, O lords! / Appoint Yama as commander-in-chief without delay, O dwellers of heaven!"
Thus spoken to, those who were the chiefs of the gods put on their armour, / [ready] with ten thousand horses in battle, adorned with golden bells.
endowed with varied wondrous virtues, hard to reach by gods and Dānavas, / the invincible chariot of the king of gods arrived, driven by Mātali.
Yama, mounted on a buffalo, stood at the head of the army, / surrounded on all sides by a host of fierce attendants.
Filled with flames that arise at the end of a cosmic age, roaming in the sky, / the Fire-god, mounted on a goat, stood with a spear in his hand.
Pavana held a goad in his hand, having increased his great speed; / mounted on the lord of serpents was the lord of the waters, the Lord himself.
In a chariot yoked with men, the sky-roaming god who is lord of the Rākṣasas, / terrible, bearing a sharp sword, stood in the battle.
In a chariot [drawn by] great lions stood the divine overseer of wealth, armed with a mace; / and the Moon, the Sun, and the two Aśvins were endowed with fourfold armies.
Such were the generals of the king of gods, invincible in the three worlds; / and the thirty-three crores of hosts of the deities of deities [stood ready].

Upon that elephant named Airāvaṇa, resembling the Himācala, with white and lovely chowries, garlanded with pure, beautiful golden lotuses, / made delightful with blazing shoots of saffron, crowded with playful swarms of bees on its temples,
sat [Indra], high-minded, wearing varied ornaments and garments, / bearing the broad thunderbolt, adorned with an excellent canopy, wearing sprawling armlets resembling coiled serpents,
the thousand-eyed one whose sprout-like feet were praised, the ruler of heaven, Pākaśāsana. / Crowded with troops of horses and herds of elephants, adorned with white parasols and banners,
there shone that invincible array of foot soldiers, impassable with warriors of diverse weapons. / Then the two Aśvins, the Maruts, along with the Sādhyas and Purandara,
Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Gandharvas, with varied divine weapons in hand, / of great strength, gathering all together, struck at the lord of the Daityas.
Yet the weapons did not even take effect upon his body resembling a mountain of adamantine rock. / Then, leaping down from his chariot, Tāraka, sovereign of the Dānavas,
slew the gods by the crores with his bare hands and heels; / and the remaining forces of the gods fled in all directions.
Terrified, abandoning their quarters and their equipment of war, / seeing those gods fleeing, Tāraka spoke these words:
"Do not kill the gods, O Daityas! Let them be brought swiftly to the palace / and shown to Vajrāṅga; let him see the gods bound!"
Then the Daitya bound the guardians of the world in battle, headed by Indra / and accompanied by the Rudras, with very firm bonds, like a herdsman binding cattle.

Mounting his chariot again, he went to his own abode, / on the vast mountain peak resounding with Siddhas and Gandharvas,

being praised by the sons of Diti, well served by the Apsarases.
